newsitem.title: FRANCE: Depp true to rebel soul in Cannes director debut.
newsitem.headline: Depp true to rebel soul in Cannes director debut.

text.p: Hollywood rebel Johnny Depp has stepped behind the camera for his debut film as director, sharing acting honours with Marlon Brando in a Luciferian love story.
"The Brave", shown in competition at the Cannes festival on Saturday, shows Depp as Raphael, a native American determined to pull his family out of their hovel in a California rubbish dump.
Brando, as a maker of underground "snuff films", gives him the opportunity, but the price is life itself -- Raphael must promise to die for the camera.
The part had been written with Brando in mind but Depp, 33, had never dared speak of the role to his friend and mentor, with whom he had acted on "Don Juan DeMarco".
It was Brando himself who volunteered for the role on the first day of shooting.

"Raphael is given an opportunity to make a lot of money. But he's in a Catch 22. It's not even important whether he does it or not. What is important is the potential for the last seven days of his life," the Kentucky-born Depp said.

The film itself was almost still-born. Aziz Ghazal, director of "Before and After", optioned the story from thriller writer Gregory McDonald, but in December 1993 Ghazal killed his ex-wife and daughter before shooting himself. Producers stuck to the project and hired Depp.
"To cleanse the film of its history and its past, and to give us a good send-off, I had (Indian activist) Floyd 'Red Crow' Westerman perform a sunrise ceremony" to bless the film, remembered Depp.
A stifling yellow light weighs on the rubbish dump as Depp slowly spins out his last days to a score written by Iggy Pop.
Raphael surprises his family and friends with adoring and expensive gifts, only to be accused of returning to his previous life of crime.
"I should be committed to an institution for even thinking that I could get away with this," Depp said.

"As a director, you have to be in complete control of the set and the surroundings. As an actor, you have to be, in a sense, out of control and unaware of what's going on on the set, and all those really fun production problems," he said.

Both Brando and Al Pacino have dubbed Depp the best actor of his generation. "I don't know why people like that say those things but I mean, obviously, that's great. I'm lucky to be able to say that they are friends of mine, but they are heroes too, you know," Depp told an interviewer recently.

Depp, who settled in Los Angeles in his teens in hopes of a career in music, will meet former jury president Sydney Pollack in Cannes to discuss a planned $40 million production of Graham Greene's "The Quiet American".
Industry sources said Depp may star in the espionage story alongside Sean Connery, who has already signed up for the movie to be directed by Phillip Noyce.
